title: addition and subtraction of decimals to hundredths

lesson.title: Adding and Subtracting Decimals — Snack Shop Math

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Imagine it's snack day at your school here in BC. You grab a granola bar that costs one dollar and twenty-five cents, and a juice box that costs two dollars and forty cents. Before you get to the till, you want to know one thing: how much is that altogether? That's exactly why we learn to add decimals — money and measuring are full of them.

visual.caption: Two prices we want to put together

steps.say: First, let's remember what those two little digits after the dot mean. One whole dollar can be cut into one hundred pennies. So this big square is one dollar, cut into one hundred tiny squares. When I shade twenty-five of them, that's twenty-five hundredths — a quarter, twenty-five cents. The second digit after the dot is always the hundredths place.

visual.caption: 25 shaded out of 100 squares means 0.25, or 25 cents

steps.say: Now here's my favourite habit: guess before you add. One dollar twenty-five is close to one dollar. Two dollars forty is close to two dollars. One plus two is three, so our answer should land near three dollars. If we ever get something silly like thirty-six dollars, we'll know right away that something went wrong.

visual.caption: Our estimate: the answer should sit near 3

steps.say: Here's the one big rule for decimals: line up the dots. When the decimal points sit right on top of each other, the pennies land under the pennies and the dollars land under the dollars. Five hundredths plus zero hundredths is five hundredths. Two tenths plus four tenths is six tenths. One plus two is three. So the total is three dollars and sixty-five cents — and look, that's right near our guess of three dollars. Perfect.

Now you hand the cashier a five dollar bill. How much change do you get back? Instead of borrowing and regrouping, let's just hop up the number line. From three dollars sixty-five, hop thirty-five cents to get to four dollars even. Then hop one whole dollar to reach five. Thirty-five cents plus one dollar is one dollar thirty-five. Let's check it: three sixty-five plus one thirty-five is five dollars exactly. It works!

visual.caption: Hop up from 3.65 to 5.00 — the jump is 1.35

steps.say: Let's try one with metres now. You planted a sunflower and measured it at zero point six eight metres. Two weeks later it grew another zero point four five metres. Here's a lovely thinking trick: zero point six eight needs thirty-two more hundredths to make one whole metre. So take thirty-two from the forty-five, which leaves thirteen. One whole metre and thirteen hundredths. Your sunflower is one point one three metres tall.

visual.caption: 0.68 plus 32 hundredths fills one whole metre

steps.say: Let's see that sunflower on the number line so it really sticks. We start at zero point six eight, jump forward zero point four five, and land at one point one three metres — a bit past one metre. And does that feel sensible? Zero point six eight is about seven tenths, zero point four five is about half. Seven tenths plus a half is a little over one. Yes, our answer fits beautifully.

visual.caption: The sunflower grows from 0.68 m to 1.13 m

steps.say: So remember this, and decimals will never scare you: guess first, line up the dots, then add or subtract just like whole numbers. Dollars under dollars, pennies under pennies. You've got this!

lesson.answer: Line up the decimal points, then add or subtract like normal — and always estimate first to check your answer makes sense.

practice.question: At the school market you buy an apple for $0.85 and a muffin for $2.35. You pay with a $5 bill. How much do the snacks cost altogether, and how much change do you get back?
